description: I’m a developer and storyteller who loves turning space science into games anyone can play. My skills: web development (HTML/JS), Python and data, game design, pixel-art visuals and video. This year we’re building a kid-friendly game about hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Join us if you love space, learning by playing, or making science feel simple. We’d love teammates with skills in sound design, pixel art, or science writing.
summary:
We made a small browser game about the things NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. You drive a rover by holding one arrow button.

Kids don’t read the story. They find it.

On the Moon you’re in the Apollo 15 rover, looking for five things the astronauts left, like the bottom half of the lander and a laser mirror that still works. On Mars you’re Opportunity. It was only meant to last 90 days and kept going for about 14 years, until a giant dust storm in 2018. You find four pieces from its landing, and then the storm comes.

Every time you find something, a short card tells you what it was and why it mattered. The cards go into an album you can open at the end to read more about each one. There’s also a quiz: it describes what a part did, and you guess which part it is.

It works on phones and computers with no download. It’s made for kids, but it only takes a few minutes to play.
details:
Still Here is a free pixel game for kids, playable on phone or PC with no download. Players drive the Apollo 15 rover on the Moon and the Opportunity rover on Mars with one arrow button, and find the hardware NASA left behind: 5 pieces on the Moon and 4 on Mars. Each find opens a short card in simple words about what the piece did and why it mattered. Cards go into an album, and the Album Hall lets players tap any card and read more with a source link. Finishing a chapter earns a mission patch.

Benefit and impact: it turns the story of left-behind hardware into something kids discover themselves, so they learn real NASA history and science while playing. Opportunity’s story (built for 90 Mars days, worked about 14.5 years) shows kids how missions end and why they matter.

Tools: HTML5, JavaScript and the Phaser 3 game library, with original pixel art and sound. Facts come from NASA Apollo records, NASA/JPL Opportunity pages, HiRISE imagery and NASA’s Heat Shield Rock page.

Creative approach: one button, no reading walls, and a warm tone: left behind, still here, never forgotten. We designed it to work on small screens and for young players.
